b: With Mouse, Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson have made their third coming-of-age story. These artistic and life partners have carved out a niche with their tender portraits of characters coming into their sense of self and an accompanying awareness of those around them. However, after a pair of movies where that self-discovery happens later in life, Mouse is their first film centered on the genre’s usual subject: a teenager.

Set in 2002, Mouse draws on O’Sullivan’s experiences growing up in Little Rock, where she endured a tragedy similar to the one that befalls the film’s protagonist. The withdrawn Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer) finds her world upended when her longtime best friend, the sociable Callie (Chloe Coleman), dies suddenly in a car accident. That loss leaves Minnie reeling and isolated until she finds an unexpected companion in grief: Callie’s mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo), a British-born former concert pianist who no longer has an anchor in Arkansas.

Minnie’s journey through her grief still intersects with many familiar, if well-drawn, figures from the genre, such as a new crush (Iman Vellani’s Kat), a perceptive teacher (David Hyde Pierce’s Mr. Murdaugh), two peer rivals (Audrey Grace Marshall’s Cara and Addisyn Grace Cain’s Brandi), and her own compassionate but cantankerous mother (Tara Mallen’s Barbara). Yet it’s the unlikely bond that forms between Minnie and Helen—not quite friends, not just surrogate mother and daughter—that comes to define Mouse. This nebulous but authentically human relationship mirrors the jumbled nature of the grieving process itself.

I spoke with O’Sullivan and Thompson on the eve of Mouse’s theatrical release. Our chat covered how they create empathy through their filmmaking process, why intergenerational friendships are a staple of their work, and how the teenage soul stays the same across time.
Your work has such a grace that I almost don’t want to demystify it, but how and where are you building such empathy for your characters into the process?
Alex Thompson: It starts with you, Kelly, and the script. But we think about it a lot.

Kelly O’Sullivan: In my writing, I’m actually trying to grant the world the empathy that I struggle with, so it’s very active. The way that we think about it is that we always want the circumstances to be the antagonist, and that everybody is doing the best that they can, but nobody knows how in the really hard moments in life. It does start from that place of trying to grant everyone the grace that’s really hard to find in life.

AT: You can have a version of omniscience as a filmmaker, where you know and understand that Cara isn’t as bad as she seems. When we’re working with Audrey, we weren’t talking about Cara the villain or the mean girl. We were talking about her experience with grief. I remember moments in our earlier work where we both felt like we didn’t draw a person with enough complexity. I don’t think everything has to be woo-woo or that everyone has to be redeemed. It’s that we’re all complex, and it makes the film more complex when you let in those gray areas.
KO: Letting people be as wonderful and as terrible as they are in life.
You remind me of a quote from my favorite movie, Annie Hall: “You’re always trying to get things to come out perfect in art because it’s real difficult in life.”
KO: Exactly, and there’s a bit of wanting to model how we can lean on each other. Connection is—and I say this as a person who sometimes struggles with connection—the only way through.

Kelly, how did you step outside some of the personal experiences that informed the core of Mouse and build in these beautiful moments with the adults? I think of the shame that Barbara feels when she realizes she’s invaded her daughter’s privacy during an intimate moment, or Mr. Murdaugh’s recognition that he needs to let Minnie work through her feelings on stage, even if the number is a bit of a train wreck. Teens so often don’t have that perception of the adults in their lives.

KO: Unfortunately, I’m an adult now, as much as I keep trying to deny it. I’m in my 40s, and whenever I think of myself as being a kid, then I actually interact with an 18-year-old, and I’m like, “Oh, I’m very different and very far away from that now.” I see where adults are coming from, and especially now, being a parent, you understand how impossible it is. That’s where all of my love for the Barbara character comes from. She’s doing the best that she can, but from a teenage point of view, of course she’s mortifying and embarrassing. Of course you’d want to go over to Helen’s house rather than Barbara’s house. But from an adult point of view, you really get where Barbara’s coming from. I feel like I’ve lived both sides of it now. I remember that teenage frustration, but I’m also in the teacher and parent shoes now.

AT: Something I never thought about, even when we were making Mouse, because our child was quite young, is that there’s no energy to spare for not being mortifying. That’s not a priority. There’s no time to be a cool parent. Barbara can’t begin to address the fact that Minnie is mortified by her. She’s too busy parenting and being a full person in the world.

This is somewhat unusual among coming-of-age stories, at least ones about teenagers, because most of Minnie’s relationships in the film are with adults. While there’s a central love story with a peer, how did this dynamic emerge and develop into such a focus of Mouse?

KO: It started as this idea of a trio with Callie in the middle and then these supporting characters in the background, people who’ve devoted their whole lives to being backup to her, both Minnie and Helen in different ways. Then, what would it be like if Callie were gone? How do those two people fall together? I wasn’t even really thinking about it in terms of peers versus adult relationships. It was the relationship that felt the most interesting to me, and of course there’s what we come to learn, which is that it’s not the same for them. Losing a friend isn’t the same as losing a child. But, for a while, they’re [both] unconsciously trying to replace Callie.

AT: I like the stickiness, too, of Helen and Minnie. That was always the moment in the script where I felt like, “Oh, this is a movie.” Helen’s presence, and the fact that it perhaps isn’t the right choice for either of them, felt deeply interesting. I haven’t really seen that before. I find the comparisons to Lady Bird interesting. I really like Lady Bird, and I think we have a similar mother-daughter relationship with Barbara and Minnie. But the fulcrum of the plot and the choices that these characters [are much different]. I love the world that Kelly has built around grief, and the way that we try to repress it, wash over it, or move through it. I think there’s a lot of wisdom there. Not that there isn’t wisdom in Lady Bird, but it’s such a different dynamic.

Intergenerational friendships and relationships are such a rarity in cinema, as in life, and there’s something thrilling—but, I imagine, also challenging—about how few standard narrative frameworks there are for them.

AT: What’s great about making movies is that you work like hell on the script to make it a document that can withstand pressure, and then you’re responding to what’s on the monitor every day and in every take. What you get with performers like Katherine and Sophie is this deep well of real-life complexity, not performed complexity or the affectation of depth. You get to watch these scenarios that Kelly has rendered so beautifully on the page play out in a thousand different directions. Maybe it’s challenging when we talk about the movie before it’s been made. But once you start making it, your reference point becomes the film itself, and this was such a gratifying movie to make because there was something to discover every day.

KO: I’m thinking about what you said about intergenerational friendships, and I’m realizing it’s in everything I’ve ever written. In Saint Frances, there’s a three-generation story with the mom going through postpartum depression. There’s also the lead character’s own mother. There are all these generations of women talking to each other and sharing experiences. I won’t even say wisdom, because I think the thing that’s true throughout is that the older generations are struggling just as much as the younger generations. That’s something that makes writing really fun, going back to this idea that nobody knows what they’re doing, no matter how old you are.

I feel like I’m just a quote machine today, but I think Lindsey Graham, of all people, made a smart observation about this: “When I was first elected to the House, I looked for the they who run things. What I finally realized is there is no they. There is only we, and we usually don’t know what the fuck we’re doing.”

KO: Obama has a very similar quote where he was like, “I kept thinking that I would be meeting these really smart people as I ascended through the political sphere.” And then he was like, “And then you realize that the people in these high positions don’t know what they’re doing.”
AT: [laughs] I appreciate the pivot to Obama from Woody Allen and Lindsey Graham.

Setting the film in 2002 means reckoning with the different ways people experience and perform grief. Some of the shifts are obvious, like cellphones and social media warping the teenage experience. But did anything surprise you that might not have changed as much as we’d think?

KO: Chloe Coleman said the teenage soul stays the same, no matter the time period or generation. I found that refreshing and comforting. When it comes to relationships and the teen experience of first love, or loss, or feeling like an outsider, that feels unchanged. We have a little mention of homophobia, which I think has changed…but probably not as much as we think, especially in Arkansas. But aside from the cellphones and the technology, a lot of it is the same.
How did you describe the Little Rock of 2002 to the cast? The sense of place feels unique and distinct, but I assume that had to be articulated.

KO: The nice thing was that we shot in Arkansas. I didn’t have to explain much other than talking about how I didn’t know anybody in my high school who was out, and how different that is now. We talked about the undercurrent of Christianity being part of the soup that you grow up in, but we let them be in that space and absorb it. We cast a lot of locals, and through having true Arkansans in the film, Katherine was immersed in it all. Chloe, Sophie, David, and others who aren’t from there were immersed in it with people who live there.

There’s an interesting yin and yang between Ghostlight and Mouse, especially in how they relate to the theater. In one, it’s a way of becoming oneself; in the other, a way of escaping oneself. In one, the performers get to be good through some of the amateurishness; in the other, maybe not so much. Since their development processes were somewhat intertwined, was one informing the other?

KO: I’m glad you picked up on that, because you’d be surprised how many people are like, “They’re both theater movies! They’re both about grief!” and only notice how they’re the same. But I think those differences are important. The way they feed into each other is that I grew up doing theater. I’m a theater kid and a theater actor. So when I’m pulling from my own experience, which I often am as a way to get to specificity, it’s part of how I understand the world. Doing theater was a huge part of my experience of high school, so that’s why it’s there. But the theater world is Callie’s world, so Minnie is going to move even farther away from it and find something totally her own. In Ghostlight, it’s not his world, but Dan moves toward it. [Theater] can be both a terrifying thing and an incredibly comforting thing, a place where you realize maybe you do want to become somebody else and a place where you get to be yourself.
How do you approach filming theatrical performance for cinema? There’s such a delicate balance between capturing what the creative expression means for the artist and how the audience receives it.

AT: It’s very boring, but you have characters who are watching, and so you photograph from their point of view, from the audience and the wings. We privilege those points of view, and those feel a little bit more objective. The subjectivity comes from what they’re feeling and what they’re giving the camera. For Minnie’s performance, and to a much lesser degree Cara and Brandi’s performance, we chose to put the camera up on stage and privilege the emotional experience of performing. The contortionist, the magician, the tap dancer—they don’t get that same treatment. We always start from who’s watching and whose point of view is important.

For instance, in the drama classroom, there’s an objectivity to the way we shot that on the zoom lens, just to offset the potential for it to feel like a heavy-handed moment. We were very conscious that it could be extraordinarily on the nose if we did it wrong, and so we basically were like, “Oh, this is sort of a doc. This is like D.A. Pennebaker’s Original Cast Album: Company.” We shot that and then caught David watching in that moment, almost by accident. It’s actually a freeze frame. It’s like six frames per second because we didn’t have enough, so we slowed it down. We focus on who’s watching and what they’re supposed to be getting out of it.
